hints: Split the job: if you knew you take i tiles from a and k - i from b, could you solve each row on its own and then combine them?

Three pieces: a monotonic decreasing stack picks the best t digits from one row, a greedy merge combines two sequences (compare the remaining suffixes, not just the front digits), and you try every valid split i.

1. For each i from max(0, k - b.length) to min(k, a.length):
  2. Best i digits of a: stack, pop smaller tops while you can still afford to drop digits.
  3. Best k - i digits of b the same way.
  4. Merge: repeatedly take from the sequence whose remaining suffix is lexicographically larger.
  5. Keep the largest merged result.

approaches.name: Brute force
approaches.idea: Try every way to choose k tiles across both rows and every interleaving, keeping the largest sequence.

approaches.name: Optimal
approaches.idea: For every split, pick the best digits from each row with a monotonic stack and merge greedily by comparing suffixes; keep the best of all splits.
approaches.time: O(k · (m + n + k²)) worst case (suffix comparisons in the merge)

explain: For a = [4,9,1], b = [8,2,6,3], k = 4, try splits i = 0..3. With i = 1, the best single digit of a is [9] and the best three of b are [8,6,3] (the 2 is popped when 6 arrives). Merging gives [9,8,6,3]. The other splits give [8,2,6,3], [9,8,6,1] and [8,4,9,1], so [9,8,6,3] wins. In the merge, ties matter: with [6,7] and [6,0,4], comparing only the front digits is not enough, so compare the whole remaining suffixes and take from the larger one.
recognize: Pick k digits keeping relative order to form the largest number → monotonic stack per row, plus trying every split and a greedy merge.
